case_studies.title: Built to Remember, Shipped to Forget: Operational Contracts, Failures, and Repairs in Containerized LLM Agent Deployments
case_studies.abstract: LLM agent systems reach production as container images run by platforms such as Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes. Framework and platform document opposite expectations: to the platform a container is disposable, while the framework persists conversations, pauses runs for human input, and resumes interrupted work from saved state; each side specifies only its own behavior, so the obligations their composition creates are stated nowhere. We present the first empirical study of this boundary, stating these obligations as operational contracts: guarantees a deployment must provide to preserve an agent system's required behavior when a deployment-platform event occurs. From the first-party documentation of LangGraph and the three platforms we derive 14 contracts and evaluate them with three independent sources of evidence: 433 deployed open-source agent systems, seven events induced on 12 of them, and 122 developer repairs mined from 39,261 commits, pull requests, and issues. At least one contract applies to 75.5% of the systems, yet its guarantee is routinely missing: of systems that must keep state beyond the process, 37.4% lose it to a restart and 41.5% to a container replacement, and every assessable deployment stops the framework's production server mid-drain. Induced events turn 14 of 16 predicted violations into runtime failures and all seven predicted holds pass. The failures are born in deployment but repaired in code: developer repairs independently cover twelve of the fourteen contracts, 78% change application code, and only two in three fully restore the violated guarantee. The 14-contract catalogue, detection rules, fault-injection harness, and 35-pattern repair taxonomy provide a basis for checking and strengthening agent deployments.
case_studies.summary: This study maps 14 operational contracts that must hold when running LLM agent containers on Docker, Compose or Kubernetes, and shows that many deployments miss these guarantees, causing state loss and failures. The authors provide a catalogue, detection rules, a fault‑injection tool and a taxonomy of 35 repair patterns to help detect and fix such issues. For most IT infrastructure teams, the findings are highly relevant because they expose hidden dependencies between container lifecycle events and agent state management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage containerised LLM agents, check your platform and framework documentation for the 14 contracts; use the supplied detection rules to scan your deployments for missing guarantees; and apply the 35 repair patterns to fix state‑loss or interruption failures before they hit production.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses operational contracts for containerized LLM agent deployments, directly impacting how IT engineers manage state persistence, failure handling, and deployment practices in Kubernetes/Docker environments. It provides empirical evidence, a contract catalogue, detection rules, and repair patterns that can be adopted or adapted by practitioners. While the research is mature (published with empirical data and tooling), it is still an academic study rather than a ready-to-deploy product, so the maturity score reflects that. The monetisation potential is moderate: engineers could incorporate these contracts and repair patterns into their CI/CD pipelines or offer consulting services on agent deployment reliability, but it is not an off-the-shelf SaaS offering. Thus the total score is 55 out of 75.

case_studies.title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
case_studies.abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the issue of keeping autonomous robots’ self‑developed goals aligned with human intentions. The authors built a multimodal system that uses large language and vision models to turn natural‑language user goals into robot missions and drives, then tests it in simulation and on a real robot, showing that the robots produce valid, aligned behaviours.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on aligning autonomous robots using LLMs and VLMs, which is outside the typical IT infrastructure concerns of the target audience. The system is demonstrated in simulation and a single physical robot, indicating limited practical deployment. No evidence of released code or scalable tooling that an IT engineer could adopt or sell within 90 days. Thus, the impact, maturity, and monetisation potential are modest.

case_studies.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents
case_studies.abstract: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.
case_studies.summary: AgentProofBench provides a benchmark for reusable verification of web agents, linking acceptance rules to execution outcomes across many tasks and services. It builds a dataset of 97 tasks, 79 families, and four web services, and shows that reusable verification can maintain high correctness rates. The study offers a concrete baseline for measuring verification quality, which is relevant for managing cloud‑based AI services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI services, use AgentProofBench to test your verification rules against real execution scenarios: 1) Run the benchmark tests to evaluate your rule compliance; 2) Compare your system’s success rates to the reported 82/96 and 79/96 scores; 3) Adjust your verification logic if your rates fall below the baseline to improve reliability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a benchmark for verifying web agents, which is a niche area with limited direct impact on current IT infrastructure workflows. The methodology and datasets are available, indicating some maturity, but it is primarily a research benchmark rather than a deployable system. There is no clear immediate commercial application that an IT engineer could adopt or sell within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence: Supply Chain Deployment
case_studies.abstract: Industrial spatial decisions are assembled across systems that share neither a reference frame nor an owner, and analysts spend substantial effort reconciling those systems rather than reasoning about space. This paper presents ANASSA, a reference architecture integrating structured reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, authoritative spatial grounding, and feedback-driven execution, and reports its instantiation in an operating supply-chain deployment. The architecture places typed data contracts at agent boundaries, validates spatial claims against a certified authoritative foundation, and enforces two blocking human-in-the-loop approvals inside a six-step cognitive loop. The deployment covers multi-hazard risk assessment on an ocean-and-inland freight lane, including cold-chain excursion detection over container telemetry. Across a three-month proof of concept (POC) with three implementation iterations, three deployment outcomes are reported: 25% improvement in data quality, 50% reduction in spatial workflow runtime, and 60% lower decision latency relative to the preceding manual workflow. Absolute deployment-scale quantities and baseline counts are confidential; reported percentages are observed relative changes. These are uncontrolled deployment observations, not controlled experiments. We therefore specify instrumentation and ablation protocols for mechanism-level evaluation.
case_studies.summary: ANASSA is a cloud‑based orchestration framework that pulls together spatial data from unrelated systems, validates it against an authoritative source, and enforces human approvals. In a supply‑chain test it cut data‑quality issues by 25 %, sped up spatial workflows by 50 %, and lowered decision latency by 60 %.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for spatial or supply‑chain services, deploy ANASSA as a micro‑service layer: 1) define typed data contracts at agent boundaries, 2) integrate an authoritative spatial database for claim validation, 3) embed the two human‑approval checkpoints in your workflow orchestration engine.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper describes a specialized agentic orchestration framework for spatial intelligence in supply chain logistics. While it reports measurable improvements, the scope is narrow to spatial decision workflows in a specific industrial context. It offers no ready-to-deploy tooling or APIs that IT engineers in typical Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, JumpCloud, Okta, AWS, Azure, or endpoint management environments can immediately adopt. The system is still at a proof‑of‑concept stage, with no released code or open‑source components. Monetisation potential is limited because the framework would require significant adaptation to fit other domains and no commercial product or service is presented. Overall, the direct relevance and practical applicability to the target IT audience are low.
